newsitem.title: PERU: Peru attack plan would end crisis in seven minutes.
newsitem.headline: Peru attack plan would end crisis in seven minutes.

text.p: U.S. and Peruvian commandos would drop onto the roof of the Japanese ambassador's home on a moonless night, plant explosives and end Latin America's longest hostage siege in minutes, according to a military memorandum.

But the Peruvian military plan, as outlined in an army intelligence memorandum obtained on Monday by Reuters, would carry a heavy cost in lives, with casualties as high as 90 people, including three-quarters of the 72 men being held by Marxist rebels, most of the hostage-takers and 20 commandos.
The military card, therefore, should only be played if negotiations fail, said the memo, dated Feb. 5 and addressed to Armed Forces chief army Gen. Nicholas de Bari Hermoza Rios.
"It is recommended that military action be left as a last resort," it said.
President Alberto Fujimori, meanwhile, denied the government intended to carry out such a plan.
"That there will be such a violent entry ... is totally false," Fujimori told reporters during a trip to Peru's northeastern Amazon jungle province of Loreto.
"But I repeat, we do not discard the possibility of a forceful intervention in the case that we have already explained," he added.
Fujimori has said the government will only use force to end the 62-day hostage crisis if a hostage is harmed. He said the government would continue seeking a peaceful solution.

But the preparation of a military option to end the crisis has been known since early in the siege. Details of the operation were published for the first time on Sunday in a local daily, La Republica, and confirmed by Reuters on Monday.

About 15 rebels of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) stormed a cocktail party and seized the diplomatic compound on Dec. 17, taking hundreds of VIPs hostage and demanding the release of 400 jailed comrades, which Fujimori has flatly rejected.
All but 72 mostly middle-aged men have been released.
Experts speculated the military plan was leaked to spur talks aimed at peacefully ending the crisis, which appeared bogged down on Saturday after three face-to-face meetings.

"Is this an attempt by the government to pressure the MRTA to drop its demand for the freedom of its prisoners, and a threat that the government has prepared a military plan in case the peaceful option fails?" La Republica's publisher Gustavo Mohme asked in a column.
"There is still a favourable outlook ... for a peaceful solution to the crisis," the army memo said.

The document said Fujimori might consider releasing "some MRTA prisoners," including those sentenced for supplying logistic support to the MRTA, for supporting subversion or for conducting intellectual work for the group.
"If it is necessary to free some prisoners, that should be done," it said.

The U.S. government has officially limited itself to statements of support for Fujimori's government. But Peruvian security force sources say U.S. security experts have been advising the government since the outset and offered to supply equipment and troops in the event of a military operation.

The U.S. embassy in Lima had no immediate comment on the plan, but said the United States weeks ago had offered the Peruvian government the help of advisers familiar with similar situations elsewhere.
According to the plan, the attack may be preceded by a city-wide blackout on a new-moon night.

Paratroopers, including U.S. commandos of Hispanic origin, would be dropped onto the roofs and patio of the residence accompanied by music played at high-volume from speakers already set up outside the compound to distract the rebels.
Commandos would then place explosives at six points around the perimeter of the compound and paratroopers would take the second floor in a bid to protect as many hostages as possible.
"A period of seven minutes is foreseen for the insurrectionary force to be annihilated," the memo said.
